title: A/B Testing Emails: What to Test and How to Measure Results

facts.fact: The article states that in email marketing, open rates can hover anywhere from 20-30%.
facts.quote: In email marketing, where open rates can hover anywhere from **20-30%**, even a tiny improvement can have an outsized impact as your list grows.

facts.fact: In an example test the article describes, two subject lines were sent to a group of 4,000 subscribers.
facts.quote: I saw a test once where a brand sent two subject lines to a group of **4,000** subscribers.

facts.fact: In the article's described test, the subject line '[Sale] Get Our Products For 50% Off' reached a 13.25% open rate.
facts.quote: The first, **"[Sale] Get Our Products For 50% Off"**, hit a **13.25% open rate**.

facts.fact: In the article's described test, the subject line 'Sale: Get Our Products For 50% Off' reached a 12.5% open rate.
facts.quote: The second, **"Sale: Get Our Products For 50% Off"**, only got a **12.5% open rate**.

facts.fact: The article reports that using brackets instead of a colon in the subject line created a 0.75% uplift in the described test.
facts.quote: That tiny change (using brackets instead of a colon) created a **0.75%** uplift.

facts.fact: The author states that in their experience, for almost any email with a commercial goal, a button outperforms a text link about 9 times out of 10.
facts.quote: for almost any email with a commercial goal, a button wins **9 times out of 10**.

facts.fact: In one analysis cited by the author, a simple CTA variant test raised click-through rate from 2.5% to 3.2%, a 28% relative increase.
facts.quote: a simple CTA variant test boosted the click-through rate from **2.5% to 3.2%**

facts.fact: The article describes 95% confidence level as the industry standard target for email A/B test statistical significance.
facts.quote: The industry standard is to aim for a **95% confidence level**.

facts.fact: At a 95% confidence level, the article says there is only a 5% probability that the observed difference was due to pure chance.
facts.quote: there's only a **5%** probability that the difference you saw was due to pure chance.

facts.fact: The article's first rule is to run an email A/B test for at least 24 hours.
facts.quote: **Run it for at least 24 hours.**

facts.fact: The article's rule of thumb is to let an email test run for 48-72 hours or until statistical significance is reached, whichever takes longer.
facts.quote: let a test run for **48-72 hours**, or until you reach statistical significance, whichever takes longer.

facts.fact: The article recommends sending each version of an email A/B test to at least 1,000 subscribers.
facts.quote: try to send each version of your test to at least **1,000 subscribers**.

facts.fact: For a simple two-version email A/B test, the article says the test segment needs 2,000 people.
facts.quote: that means you'll need a test segment of 2,000 people.

facts.fact: Adwave says its campaigns are available for as little as $30 per day.
facts.quote: campaigns available for as little as **$30/day**

facts.fact: Adwave says its TV advertising can place an ad on over 100 premium channels.
facts.quote: You can get your ad on over 100 premium channels, blanketing your local market

facts.fact: The article recommends letting an email A/B test run for at least 24 hours.
facts.quote: I always recommend letting a test run for at least **24 hours**

facts.fact: The article recommends at least 1,000 subscribers per variation for an email A/B test.
facts.quote: you really want at least **1,000 subscribers per variation** to get a result you can trust

facts.fact: The article states that a 50/50 split of a 1,000-subscriber list gives each version a 500-person audience.
facts.quote: a 50/50 split gives each version a 500-person audience

facts.fact: The article describes the industry standard statistical significance confidence level as 95%.
facts.quote: The industry standard is a **95% confidence level**

facts.fact: The article gives a 10% difference in clicks between two versions as an example that may still be random noise if the list is small.
facts.quote: Just because Version A got **10%** more clicks than Version B doesn't mean it’s the better email.
